Redwood Inference's end-to-end process for rotating secrets and credentials used by production services (including emergency rotation) involves a repeatable procedure for rotating production secrets used by Redwood services. It covers both planned and emergency rotation patterns. [S2]

> # Purpose
> This runbook provides a repeatable procedure for rotating production secrets used by Redwood services. It covers both planned and emergency rotation patterns.

The process includes identifying the secret name/path and all consumers, confirming rotation type (planned vs emergency), and ensuring appropriate access (normal approvals or break-glass for emergencies). [S3]

> # Preconditions
> - Identify the secret name/path and all consumers (see Credential Dependencies page).
> - Confirm rotation type: planned vs emergency.
> - Ensure appropriate access (normal approvals or break-glass for emergencies).

The rotation patterns include dual-valid window (preferred) and cutover (use with caution). Dual-valid window is used when the downstream system can accept two credentials temporarily, while cutover is used when only one credential can be active. [S4]

> # Rotation patterns
> ## Pattern A: Dual-valid window (preferred)
> Use when the downstream system can accept two credentials temporarily (e.g., JWT verification keys, API keys with overlap).

Emergency rotation during an active incident involves a coordinated process for rotating secrets quickly. It includes declaring in incident channel, linking break-glass event, identifying rotation order, and validating per-service health. [S11]

> # Goal
> Provide a coordinated process for rotating secrets quickly during an active incident (suspected compromise or immediate containment need).

The emergency rotation procedure includes steps such as declaring in incident channel, identifying rotation order, and validating per-service health. It also involves roles like Incident Commander, Ops/SRE, Security, and Service owners. [S14]

> # Roles
> - Incident Commander (IC): authorizes emergency rotation and prioritizes which secrets first
> - Ops/SRE: executes changes and monitors service health
> - Security: advises on scope and evidence capture
> - Service owners: update consumers and validate functionality

Mitigation steps included pausing export generation, backfilling after the fix, and resuming exports with corrected logic. > 3) Add contract test in the usage pipeline for streaming retry semantics. Owning team: Eng Platform.

Redwood Inference's end-to-end process for rotating secrets and credentials used by production services (including emergency rotation) involves defining standards for storage, usage, and rotation of secrets and credentials to reduce the blast radius of credential compromise and ensure rotation is routine and low-risk. [S1]

> # Overview
> This standard defines how Redwood Inference stores, uses, and rotates **secrets and credentials** for production services. The objective is to reduce the blast radius of credential compromise and ensure rotation is routine and low-risk.

Rotating secrets and credentials used by production services involves replacing a secret with a new value and updating all consumers, with specific requirements based on secret classification and rotation cadence. [S2]

> # Definitions
> - **Secret**: any value that grants access (API keys, database passwords, service tokens, signing keys, OAuth client secrets, private keys).
> - **Credential rotation**: replacing a secret with a new value and updating all consumers.
> - **Emergency rotation**: accelerated rotation performed due to suspected compromise or active incident.

Credentials used by production services must be stored in approved systems such as Redwood Vault or Cloud KMS/HSM-backed secret stores where required by compliance. [S3]

> # Approved storage systems
> Production secrets must be stored in one of the following:
> - Redwood Vault (primary)
> - Cloud KMS/HSM-backed secret store where required by compliance (Private deployments may vary)

Production services use secrets and credentials that are classified into tiers based on their sensitivity and access requirements. [S5]

> # Secret classification
> - **Tier 0**: root/admin credentials, signing keys, KMS master operations.
> - **Tier 1**: service-to-service auth tokens, database credentials, message bus credentials.
> - **Tier 2**: third-party API keys with limited scopes, internal read-only tokens.

Emergency rotation is an accelerated process performed during active incidents or suspected compromises, involving coordinated steps to quickly rotate secrets while ensuring service continuity. [S8]

> # Purpose
> This runbook provides a repeatable procedure for rotating production secrets used by Redwood services. It covers both planned and emergency rotation patterns.

Redwood Inference's end-to-end process for rotating secrets and credentials used by production services (including emergency rotation) involves mandatory controls and end-to-end procedures for onboarding, operating, and decommissioning third-party integrations. This includes ensuring least-privilege access, consistent audit trail, and immutable evidence. [S1]

> - In-scope: any integration that reads, writes, proxies, or requests metadata from production services, including SaaS connectors, hosted vendor agents, and partner-managed webhooks.
> - Out-of-scope: internal tools that never connect to customer or production data channels (documented exceptions require risk approval).

Secrets and credentials are rotated according to a defined schedule: Tier 0 (root/admin credentials) every 30 days, Tier 1 (service-to-service auth tokens) every 90 days, and Tier 2 (third-party API keys) every 180 days. Emergency rotation is performed if a secret is exposed or a workstation is compromised. [S11]

> # Overview
> This standard defines how Redwood Inference stores, uses, and rotates **secrets and credentials** for production services. The objective is to reduce the blast radius of credential compromise and ensure rotation is routine and low-risk.

Redwood Inference stores secrets and credentials in Redwood Vault (primary) or Cloud KMS/HSM-backed secret stores where required by compliance. Secrets are not stored in plaintext in Git repositories, Confluence/Google Docs, CI logs, or container images. [S13]

> # Approved storage systems
> Production secrets must be stored in one of the following:
> - Redwood Vault (primary)
> - Cloud KMS/HSM-backed secret store where required by compliance (Private deployments may vary)

Production services use secrets and credentials for accessing APIs, databases, and message buses. Integrations are assigned roles (read-only, write-limited, or admin-proxy) to control access. [S8]

> 1. Minimized privileged identities
> - All third-party integrations must use dedicated service identities (no shared human credentials).
> - Each connector gets a unique long-lived client-id and short-lived credential pattern when supported (preferred: OIDC + short-lived TLS or mTLS).

Emergency rotation is performed during an active incident (suspected compromise or immediate containment need) to quickly rotate secrets and ensure low-risk rotation. [S12]

> # Definitions
> - **Secret**: any value that grants access (API keys, database passwords, service tokens, signing keys, OAuth client secrets, private keys).
> - **Credential rotation**: replacing a secret with a new value and updating all consumers.
> - **Emergency rotation**: accelerated rotation performed due to suspected compromise or active incident.
